questions.title: Why was the indictment dismissed for failure to state an offense if the government alleged obvious lies in a pump-and-dump scheme?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural posture here. The defendants were indicted for securities fraud based on allegedly false social-media posts used to pump stock prices, which seems like classic fraud. But the district court still dismissed the indictment for failure to state an offense. At the indictment stage, does the court assume all factual allegations are true and only ask whether those facts match the statutory elements? If so, what exactly was the district court saying was missing here, and why did the Fifth Circuit think that was a legal error rather than just a disagreement about the facts?

questions.title: How is 'fraudulent inducement' different from the Supreme Court's rejected 'right-to-control' theory after Ciminelli?
questions.question_body: The opinion says the indictment was valid because it alleged a 'fraudulent-inducement theory,' not a 'right-to-control theory.' I'm having trouble seeing the line between them. In both situations, the victim is misled by false information when deciding whether to enter a transaction. If the followers here were tricked by false posts into buying stocks, why isn't that just depriving them of 'valuable economic information' needed to make an investment decision, which Ciminelli says is not enough? What makes this case about obtaining money or property rather than merely interfering with informed decisionmaking?

questions.title: Why does buying a security count as being deprived of money or property if the buyer receives shares in return?
questions.question_body: The Fifth Circuit says the indictment alleges a property deprivation because the followers were induced to purchase securities, meaning they parted with their money. But the followers also got stock in exchange, and the opinion even notes they may have received market-value securities. I thought fraud usually required cheating someone out of property in a more direct sense. Why is the transfer of money itself enough here, even if the victim receives something of equal or at least nonzero value in return? Is the theory that the victim's property interest lies in the money paid, the terms of the bargain, or the fact that consent was induced by fraud?

questions.title: After Kousisis, does federal fraud no longer require intent to cause economic loss to the victim?
questions.question_body: The part I'm struggling with most is the 'intent to defraud' analysis. The defendants argued they only intended to profit, not to harm their followers, and the Fifth Circuit said that distinction doesn't matter after Kousisis. Does that mean federal fraud statutes now require only intent to obtain money or property through deception, even if the defendant doesn't care whether the victim ends up worse off overall? If so, how does that fit with older formulations saying intent to defraud includes intent to cause harm? Is 'harm' now satisfied just by inducing someone to transfer money under false pretenses?

questions.title: What exactly is the property-holder in this pump-and-dump theory: the social-media followers, the market, or someone else?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly says the defendants fraudulently induced their followers to purchase securities and thereby obtained money or property. But in a pump-and-dump scheme, the defendants usually sell into a market at an inflated price, and the counterparties may not always be the exact followers who saw the posts. So whose property is the indictment really focused on? Does it matter for § 1348 whether the deceived person and the person from whom the money is obtained are the same? I'm trying to understand whether the Fifth Circuit is treating this as direct victim-to-defendant fraud or something more market-wide.

questions.title: How much of mail/wire fraud doctrine can courts import into 18 U.S.C. § 1348 securities fraud cases?
questions.question_body: The opinion says there is 'scant caselaw' on § 1348 in the Fifth Circuit, so the court borrows concepts from mail and wire fraud cases, including Ciminelli and Kousisis. Is that always appropriate? Section 1348 has two clauses and is specifically about securities, while the mail and wire fraud statutes have their own wording and history. Are courts treating § 1348 as basically a securities-specific analogue to mail/wire fraud, or are there meaningful doctrinal limits on importing those cases? I'm wondering whether the Fifth Circuit's reasoning depends on textual similarities, legislative purpose, or just precedent by analogy.
